newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Two Shanghainese vie to lead post-'97 legislature.
newsitem.headline: Two Shanghainese vie to lead post-'97 legislature.

text.p: The two people vying on Saturday to become leader of the provisional legislature that will make Hong Kong's laws after China takes over in July have come a long way from their origins in 1940s Shanghai.

Andrew Wong is president of the current elected Legislative Council, or Legco, and Rita Fan is active on Beijing's 400-member committee overseeing preparations for the British colony's July 1 transition to China.

Whoever wins faces the arduous task of leading a council whose very existence is the subject of controversy in the sensitive period ahead of the handover. Pro-democracy forces in Hong Kong have called the legislature "a sham". It meets across the Chinese border in Shenzhen to keep to Beijing's promise that two legislative bodies will not operate at the same time on Hong Kong soil. Ten signatures of nomination will be needed to confirm a candidacy.
Andrew Wong, 53, made his move into politics in 1985, one year after the Joint Declaration on returning Hong Kong was signed between Britain and China.
"I wanted to see to it that there's a smooth transfer, and if it was unsuccessful, to contain the damage," he told Reuters, chain-smoking in his spacious office in the Legco building.

A small, impeccably neat man, Wong agreed to an interview to talk about himself ahead of the selection on Saturday, but declined to discuss his views on the legislature or the myriad controversial issues connected to the impending handover.
"I decided back in 1995 (when I became Legco president) that I should no longer be active in politics. In order to satisfy the role of impartial speaker, I will have to restrain himself," he said.
He speaks with the air of a man who has said these things many times before -- he strongly believes the president should be an impartial leader, referee and "servant of the council".

It is this claim that lets him ignore the question of how he can in good conscience lead the current Legco and at the same time hold a seat on the China-backed provisional legislature and seek to be its president.
A Catholic, Wong continues to lecture in public administration at the Chinese University of Hong Kong. He has a wife and three children.
Rita Fan, 51, is well known for her loud support of Beijing after many years spent serving the colonial government, including holding an appointed position on the Executive Council, or cabinet.
A Legislative Councillor from 1983 to 1992, she is now a key player on Chinese committees overseeing such essential issues as nationality status after the handover and security.
Fan, who declined to be interviewed, feels the president will be responsible for explaining the work of the provisional legislature to the Hong Kong people and the world.

"I think if a decision has been reached by the provisional legislature, the decision would need to be promulgated, publicised and explained...this is because the very first doubt in people's minds must be whether the provisional legislature has the right to do so," she said earlier this month.
Fan is also remembered for her role as a leading campaigner against Hong Kong's acceptance of Vietnamese boat people.

Some 6,300 Vietnamese boat people remain in Hong Kong, down from a peak of about 60,000 in 1991 due to a programme of forced repatriation. China wants all Vietnamese asylum-seekers out of Hong Kong by the time of the handover.
Fan is married with two children. She recently donated one of her kidneys to her daughter.
